                    ### Question
                    A 63-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his wife because she is concerned he is having another stroke. The patient says he woke up with right-sided facial weakness and drooping. Past medical history is significant for a recent case of shingles treated with acyclovir, and a stroke, diagnosed 10 years ago, from which he recovered with no residual functional deficits. On physical examination, there is weakness and drooping of the entire right side of the face. Sensation is intact. The remainder of the physical examination is unremarkable. Which of the following additional findings would also most likely be seen in this patient?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Decreased salivation
opb. Partial hearing loss
opc. Complete loss of taste to the tongue
opd. Wrinkled forehead
ope. Expressive aphasia

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient's right-sided facial weakness and drooping suggest involvement of the facial nerve (CN VII), consistent with Bell's palsy, which can occur after a viral infection like shingles. In Bell's palsy, the entire side of the face is affected, including the forehead, which would not wrinkle due to paralysis. This rules out option 'd' (Wrinkled forehead). The facial nerve also controls salivation and taste to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, so decreased salivation (option 'a') and partial loss of taste (not complete, as in option 'c') are possible. Partial hearing loss (option 'b') can occur due to the proximity of the facial nerve to the ear structures, especially if the nerve's involvement affects the stapedius muscle, which dampens sound. Expressive aphasia (option 'e') is related to brain function, not facial nerve function, and is unlikely in this context. Therefore, the most likely additional finding in this patient is decreased salivation, aligning with the facial nerve's role in salivary gland innervation.
